nameStory: Micractinium bornhemiense gets its name from the Greek words 'mikros' meaning small and 'aktis' meaning ray, referring to the tiny radiating spines that stick out from each microscopic cell. The species name 'bornhemiense' honors the location where it was first discovered and described by scientists.
description: **[UNCERTAIN IDENTIFICATION WARNING]** Micractinium bornhemiense is a microscopic freshwater green alga that you'll never see with the naked eye - each individual cell is smaller than the width of a human hair. This tiny organism forms small colonies of 4-8 cells that float freely in pond water, with each spherical cell decorated with delicate spines radiating outward like a microscopic sea urchin. You'd need a good microscope with at least 400x magnification to spot these cellular jewels. Despite being incredibly small, these algae play an important role in freshwater ecosystems as primary producers.

idTips.label: Cell arrangement
idTips.description: Forms small colonies of typically 4-8 spherical cells clustered together, visible only under microscope magnification of 400x or higher

idTips.label: Radiating spines
idTips.description: Each cell bears multiple thin, needle-like projections extending outward from the cell wall surface

idTips.label: Cell size
idTips.description: Individual cells measure approximately 8-15 micrometers in diameter, much smaller than the period at the end of this sentence

idTips.label: Color appearance
idTips.description: Appears bright green under microscope due to chlorophyll, giving pond water a greenish tint when present in large numbers

habitat: **[UNCERTAIN]** Found floating in the water column of freshwater ponds, small lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. Prefers nutrient-rich waters and can be collected from surface water samples, especially in warmer months when algal growth is most active.

seasonality.summer: **[UNCERTAIN]** Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when conditions are optimal for photosynthesis and reproduction.
seasonality.fall: **[UNCERTAIN]** Numbers typically decline as temperatures drop and daylight decreases, though some populations may persist in protected waters.
seasonality.winter: **[UNCERTAIN]** Largely dormant or present in very low numbers, surviving harsh conditions in resistant forms or as resting stages.

funFact: **[UNCERTAIN]** Despite being invisible to the naked eye, millions of these microscopic algae can live in a single drop of pond water, and they produce oxygen through photosynthesis just like giant trees - meaning you might be breathing oxygen made by these tiny spined cells right now!
confusionNotes: **[UNCERTAIN]** Most likely confused with other small colonial green algae like Micractinium pusillum, which forms similar small cell clusters but may differ in spine arrangement or colony size - microscopic examination by an expert would be needed for definitive identification.
contextualKnowledge: This species represents the incredible microscopic diversity that exists in every New England pond and stream - there's an entire invisible world of algae, protists, and other microorganisms that most people never realize they're surrounded by, yet these organisms form the foundation of aquatic food webs.
compareHints: **[UNCERTAIN]** Compared to its close relative Micractinium pusillum, M. bornhemiense may differ in specific spine characteristics or colony formation patterns, though distinguishing between species in this genus typically requires expert microscopic analysis. Both species share the characteristic radiating spines and small colonial growth form that defines the Micractinium genus.
